<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line ltx_leqno">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation<span class="ltx_pubnotes"><span class="ltx_pubnotes_content"><span class="ltx_pubnote ltx_role_note"><span class="ltx_note_name">Note: </span>Accepted at the North East AI Agents Day 2026 workshop, Jane Street, New York City. <a href="https://ne-agents-day.github.io/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://ne-agents-day.github.io/</a></span></span></span></h1>

</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract.</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Bot detectors deployed at scale treat traffic as binary: human or bot.
This assumption breaks in a world where AI agents browse the web through
browser automation, a traffic class that is neither and that binary
classifiers structurally cannot represent.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.2" class="ltx_p">We present a three-class detection framework that correctly distinguishes
humans, bots, and AI agents, and show that the binary-vs-agent confusion
is architectural: a binary human-vs-bot detector <em id="abstract1.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">misroutes</em> agent
sessions because the label space lacks an agent class. On our controlled
benchmark, an MLP binary classifier misclassifies 39.1% of real AI
agents as human and a SAINT binary transformer misclassifies 34.5%;
adding an explicit agent class yields per-class agent F1 = 1.000 in
every one of 30 runs (3 model families <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> 10 seeds), eliminating
the gap entirely.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.3" class="ltx_p">To measure how evasion-resistant this detection is, we construct a
five-level evasion ladder that spans passive observation,
GAN-generated trajectories, and replay of real human cursor data
(<math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=2{,}299" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2,299</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=2{,}299</annotation></semantics></math> archived evasion sessions: 1,025 unmodified agent +
150 rule-based + 300 GAN + 300 GAN+ + 524 human replay). Across 10
seeds and 3 model families we observe zero agent misses in 22,990
per-seed predictions: 100% agent recall at every level, with macro-F1
95% CIs of <math id="abstract1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0.986,0.994]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0.986</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.994</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0.986,0.994]</annotation></semantics></math> (SAINT), <math id="abstract1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0.993,0.997]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0.993</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.997</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0.993,0.997]</annotation></semantics></math> (RF), and
<math id="abstract1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0.993,0.998]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0.993</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.998</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0.993,0.998]</annotation></semantics></math> (GBM). The discriminative signal is a
browser-automation artifact, not evidence of agent reasoning.
Playwright does not emit the raw pointer-move and wheel-delta streams
that a physical input device produces, and this absence signature
(no raw-event teleports before clicks, no wheel deltas, empty
pre-click mousemove tracks) survives trajectory manipulation.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.4" class="ltx_p">Exhaustive search over all <math id="abstract1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\binom{17}{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mn>17</mn><mi>k</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\binom{17}{k}</annotation></semantics></math> feature subsets
(<math id="abstract1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=1\ldots 5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=1\ldots 5</annotation></semantics></math>; 9,401 GBMs trained, with full per-class precision
and recall) shows that a handful of event-stream features recovers
strong agent detection. Two behavioral features
(<span id="abstract1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">mouse_event_rate</span>, <span id="abstract1.4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">teleport_click_ratio</span>) jointly
give 100% observed agent recall at every evasion level, with held-out
test macro-F1 of 0.926 and agent precision of 0.994; five features
lift macro-F1 to 0.991. Backward elimination finds a different
two-feature set ({<span id="abstract1.4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">mouse_event_rate</span>,
<span id="abstract1.4.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">click_duration_std</span>}) that also preserves 100% agent recall
at unit precision: the signal is redundantly encoded, and removing
<span id="abstract1.4.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">teleport_click_ratio</span> entirely leaves agent detection at
100%. The single-feature regime is degenerate. The one indicator that
flags every agent (<span id="abstract1.4.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">cursor_path_linearity</span>) does so by
collapsing the classifier to always predict “agent” (agent precision
0.33, macro-F1 0.17), a failure mode our per-level diagnostics surface
automatically. <span id="abstract1.4.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Two features robustly isolate agents; five
separate all three traffic classes at macro-F1 <math id="abstract1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\geq 0.99" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≥</mo><mn>0.99</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\geq 0.99</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>AI agent detection, feature selection, behavioral biometrics, adversarial evasion, minimal feature sets
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1. </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The way we interact with the internet is changing. For decades, web traffic fell into two categories: <em id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">humans</em> who browse with intent and motor variability, and <em id="S1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">bots</em>: custom scripts, scrapers, and automation frameworks that interact programmatically <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>)</cite>. The security industry built an entire detection ecosystem around this binary distinction: CAPTCHAs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>)</cite>, behavioral biometrics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>, <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>)</cite>, and commercial bot management platforms all ask the same question: <em id="S1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">human or not?</em></p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A third actor has now entered the web. LLM-driven agents (systems like Anthropic’s Computer Use <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>)</cite>, OpenAI’s Operator <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>)</cite>, and research frameworks such as WebArena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>)</cite>, BrowserGym <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>)</cite>, and Mind2Web <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>)</cite>) autonomously browse the web, reading pages, reasoning about content, and executing multi-step tasks through real browsers. Unlike traditional bots, agents generate trusted DOM events, adapt their behavior to page content, and pursue goals that require understanding. The distinction between who and what is on the internet is no longer binary.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Industry has begun to treat agents as a distinct traffic class. Cloudflare’s Signed Agents protocol <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>)</cite>, for instance, lets agents cryptographically self-identify so platforms can route, rate-limit, and serve each traffic class appropriately. But when agents do not declare themselves, platforms fall back on behavioral detection, which today remains binary: human or bot.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">This raises a fundamental question: <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">are agents just another kind of bot?</span> If so, existing binary detectors should catch them. We show that an MLP binary classifier lets 39.1% of AI agents through as “human,” a SAINT tabular transformer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>)</cite> lets 34.5% through, and a random forest lets 30.0% through. Only XGBoost catches every agent, and it does so via <em id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">coincidental</em> features (missing scroll events, absent raw mousemove streams before clicks, empty wheel-delta series) rather than agent-specific signals, so its detection is brittle. The gap is structural, not a matter of modeling capacity: a binary label space cannot represent a three-class world. Adding a third “agent” class eliminates the gap entirely (F1 = 1.000). We then show that the discriminative signal arises from how browser automation APIs generate events (programmatic DOM calls rather than hardware input), not from LLM reasoning cycles. That leaves a practical question: deploying 16+ behavioral features is expensive. How many do you <em id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">actually need</em>?</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We study this question in the setting of API-driven browser automation (Playwright), where agents interact with web pages through programmatic interfaces that generate trusted DOM events. We focus on Playwright because it is the dominant browser-driver substrate of the current agent ecosystem: Browser Use <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>)</cite>, Stagehand (Browserbase) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>)</cite>, Skyvern <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>)</cite>, and most LangChain/MCP browser tools dispatch their actions through Playwright or the near-identical Puppeteer/CDP path, so its DOM-event signature is what deployed web agents typically emit in practice. Our dataset comprises more than 14,000 real human sessions (CaptchaSolve30k), 5,000 synthetic bot samples across three archetypes, and 1,025 real agent sessions recorded from Claude driving Chrome via Playwright across ten web tasks grouped into five interaction types. Our contributions:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(1)</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We show that binary human–bot detectors miss a structural fraction of AI agents (MLP 39.1%, SAINT 34.5%, random forest 30.0%) and that this gap is architectural: a three-class formulation eliminates it entirely (§<a href="#S6" title="6. The Binary Detection Gap ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(2)</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We show that the discriminative signal is an API execution artifact rather than an agent cognition signal: detection survives even when agents replay real human cursor trajectories, because automation APIs still dispatch actions via programmatic DOM calls (§<a href="#S7" title="7. Evasion Ladder ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, §<a href="#S12" title="12. Discussion &amp; Conclusion ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(3)</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate robustness under five progressively stronger evasion strategies, from no evasion through GAN-generated trajectories to replay of real human cursor data, and observe 100% agent detection at all levels (§<a href="#S7" title="7. Evasion Ladder ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(4)</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We identify <span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">minimal feature subsets for practical deployment</span> through exhaustive search over <math id="S1.I1.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\binom{17}{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mn>17</mn><mi>k</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\binom{17}{k}</annotation></semantics></math> subsets (<math id="S1.I1.i4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> = 1…5; 9,401 GBMs), forward selection, and backward elimination (§<a href="#S9" title="9. Feature Subset Optimization ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>):</p>
<ul id="S1.I1.i4.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2 behavioral features</span> suffice for 100% agent recall at every evasion level with agent precision <math id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\geq" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≥</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\geq</annotation></semantics></math> 0.99: {<span id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">mouse_event_rate</span>, <span id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">teleport_click_ratio</span>} from exhaustive search, or {<span id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">mouse_event_rate</span>, <span id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">click_duration_std</span>} from backward elimination (held-out test macro-F1 0.926 and 0.904, respectively).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The <math id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> = 1 regime is degenerate: the one solo-“perfect” indicator (<span id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">cursor_path_linearity</span>) flags every agent only by collapsing the predictor to always output “agent” (agent precision = 0.33, macro-F1 = 0.17).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">5 features</span> reach macro-F1 <math id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\geq" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≥</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\geq</annotation></semantics></math> 0.99 for full three-class discrimination; 17 features reach 0.995.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The signal is redundantly encoded: removing <span id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">teleport_click_ratio</span> entirely leaves agent recall at 100% because <span id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">mouse_event_rate</span>, <span id="S1.I1.i4.I1.i4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">click_duration_std</span>, and the missingness-indicator channels absorb the signature (§<a href="#S9" title="9. Feature Subset Optimization ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>).</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">To our knowledge, this is the first work to study LLM-driven browser agents as a detection category distinct from traditional bots, and the first to perform exhaustive feature subset analysis for behavioral agent detection. We detail our dataset construction (§<a href="#S3" title="3. Dataset Construction ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>), feature engineering (§<a href="#S4" title="4. Feature Engineering ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>), model architecture (§<a href="#S5" title="5. Model Architecture ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>), and evasion methodology (Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Evasion Methodology ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>) to enable full reproducibility.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2. </span>Background &amp; Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The evolution of non-human web traffic mirrors the evolution of web interaction itself. Each generation of automated actors prompted a new generation of defenses, and each defense assumed that the actor taxonomy of its day was complete. We trace this progression to motivate why agents require a new detection category.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1. </span>The Two-Actor Web: Humans and Bots</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For most of the web’s history, non-human traffic meant <em id="S2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">bots</em>: scripts, scrapers, and automation frameworks that interact with websites programmatically. Early defenses relied on CAPTCHAs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>)</cite>, but as bots grew more sophisticated, the field shifted to behavioral biometrics: analyzing mouse dynamics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>, <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>)</cite>, keystroke patterns <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>)</cite>, and browser fingerprints <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>)</cite> to detect non-human behavior without explicit challenges. Iliou et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>)</cite> combined web server logs with mouse biometrics to detect advanced bots. Acien et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>)</cite> proposed BeCAPTCHA-Mouse, using GAN-generated synthetic mouse trajectories to harden bot detection via data augmentation. Chu et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>)</cite> showed that mouse dynamics carry discriminative signals even in online gaming. Commercial platforms (reCAPTCHA, hCaptcha, Akamai, Cloudflare, HUMAN) deploy these techniques at scale.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">All of these systems share a common assumption: traffic is either human or bot. The entire detection ecosystem, from feature design through model training to deployment thresholds, is built around this binary distinction. For two decades this worked, because the taxonomy was complete.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2. </span>The Third Actor: LLM-Driven Agents</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The emergence of LLM-driven web agents breaks this taxonomy. ReAct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>)</cite> demonstrated that language models can synergize reasoning and acting; WebGPT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>)</cite> showed browser-assisted question-answering with human feedback. These foundational ideas have spawned an ecosystem of agent frameworks (WebArena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>)</cite>, BrowserGym <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>)</cite>, Mind2Web <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>)</cite>, SeeAct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>)</cite>) and commercial products: Anthropic’s Computer Use <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>)</cite> and OpenAI’s Operator <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">What makes agents categorically different from bots? Bots follow predetermined scripts; agents <em id="S2.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">reason</em> about page content and adapt. Bots produce mechanical, repetitive interaction patterns; agents exhibit a characteristic <em id="S2.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">pause-think-act</em> cycle driven by LLM inference. Most critically, agents operate through real browsers via automation APIs (Playwright, Puppeteer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>)</cite>, Selenium <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>)</cite>), generating trusted DOM events that look nothing like the headless requests of traditional scrapers. This places agents in an uncanny middle ground for the most nuanced binary detectors: MLP fails on 39.1% of agents and SAINT fails on 34.5%, while simpler models catch them via coincidental features (§<a href="#S6" title="6. The Binary Detection Gap ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>). Either way, binary detectors cannot <em id="S2.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">route</em> agents as a distinct class, and their event-stream structure remains fundamentally non-human.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Our 39.1% (MLP) / 34.5% (SAINT) evasion result quantifies this gap. When the most nuanced binary detectors encounter agents, they classify roughly one in three as human, not because the detectors are weak but because agents genuinely do not fit the behavioral profile of bots. They are a third category that binary detectors were never designed to handle <em id="S2.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">via agent-specific signals</em>: XGBoost in our benchmark catches 100% of agents, but via coincidental features such as missing scroll events and empty mousemove streams, and such detection is brittle.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3. </span>Detection Methods: From Trees to Transformers</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given a three-class detection problem, classifier choice matters. Our problem is fundamentally tabular: given a vector of behavioral features, classify traffic as human, bot, or agent. Grinsztajn et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>)</cite> showed that tree-based models (XGBoost <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>)</cite>, Random Forest) still outperform deep learning on many tabular benchmarks, particularly with heterogeneous features and small datasets. Yet transformer-based architectures have closed this gap: SAINT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>)</cite> uses per-feature embedding with row attention and contrastive pre-training; TabTransformer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>)</cite> applies self-attention to categorical features; FT-Transformer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>)</cite> treats all features uniformly through per-feature projections; TabNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>)</cite> uses sequential attention for feature selection; and NODE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>)</cite> combines oblivious decision trees with gradient-based optimization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We choose SAINT because it is among the most vulnerable to agents in the binary setting (34.5% evasion, second only to MLP’s 39.1%) and because it learns the most nuanced decision boundaries between humans and bots, which means agents fall closest to the human side. If we can fix SAINT’s blind spot with a three-class formulation, the result is more meaningful than fixing a model that already catches agents by coincidence. We adapt SAINT with denoising pre-training and a multi-class output head (§<a href="#S5" title="5. Model Architecture ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.4. </span>Adversarial Evasion: How Hard Is It to Hide?</h3>

<div id="S2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">If agents are detectable, the natural follow-up is: can they evade? Adversarial machine learning has shown that classifiers can be fooled by crafted inputs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>, <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>)</cite>, and optimization-based attacks can defeat even defensive distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>)</cite>. In security domains, Grosse et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>)</cite> demonstrated adversarial evasion of malware classifiers.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For behavioral biometrics, evasion means generating human-like interaction patterns. GANs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>)</cite> have been used to synthesize realistic mouse trajectories <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>)</cite>, and replay attacks, where recorded human behavior is replayed verbatim, represent the theoretical ceiling for trajectory-level evasion. Our five-level evasion ladder (Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Evasion Methodology ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>) systematically escalates from no evasion through GAN-generated trajectories to direct replay of real human cursor data, testing whether detection relies on surface-level patterns (matchable) or fundamental event-stream structure (not matchable).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.5. </span>Feature Selection: How Little Can You Get Away With?</h3>

<div id="S2.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Even with robust detection, deploying 16+ features in production is expensive: each feature requires client-side instrumentation, server-side extraction, and ongoing maintenance. Feature selection, choosing the minimal subset that preserves performance, is therefore critical for deployment. The literature distinguishes three paradigms <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>)</cite>: <em id="S2.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">filter</em> methods rank features by statistical tests (e.g., mutual information <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>)</cite>); <em id="S2.SS5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">wrapper</em> methods evaluate subsets using the target classifier; and <em id="S2.SS5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">embedded</em> methods perform selection during training (e.g., LASSO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>)</cite>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For <math id="S2.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> features, exhaustive wrapper search requires evaluating <math id="S2.SS5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{n}-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{n}-1</annotation></semantics></math> subsets, which is feasible only for small <math id="S2.SS5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>. With 17 continuous features (16 base + <span id="S2.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">scroll_interval_variance</span> added after the resampler bug fix described in the Methodology), we enumerate all <math id="S2.SS5.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{k=1}^{5}\binom{17}{k}=9{,}401" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>5</mn></msubsup><mrow><mo lspace="0em">(</mo><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mn>17</mn><mi>k</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>9,401</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{k=1}^{5}\binom{17}{k}=9{,}401</annotation></semantics></math> subsets for <math id="S2.SS5.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> = 1…5, complemented by greedy forward selection and backward elimination. This gives practitioners a concrete answer: not just <em id="S2.SS5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">can</em> you detect agents, but <em id="S2.SS5.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">what is the least you need to deploy</em>?</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3. </span>Dataset Construction</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We construct a three-class dataset comprising human behavioral data, synthetic bot traffic, and real AI agent sessions. Figure <a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Scope of claims. ‣ 3. Dataset Construction ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes the data pipeline.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Scope of claims.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The bot class is sampled from literature-grounded distributions, so <em id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">three-class metrics</em> (macro-F1, the minimal feature set for three-class discrimination) should be interpreted relative to this controlled bot model. <em id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Agent detection</em>, however, is evaluated on real data for both the human and agent classes: the 39.1%/34.5% binary gap and the 100% three-class agent detection are bot-simulation-independent.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<div id="S3.F1.3" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:345.0pt;height:112.7pt;vertical-align:-0.0pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(36.3pt,-11.8pt) scale(1.26618124880298,1.26618124880298) ;"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S3.F1.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="123.11" overflow="visible" <figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>. </span><span id="S3.F1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Dataset construction pipeline. Human behavioral data from CaptchaSolve30k, synthetic bot traffic from a three-archetype generator, and real AI agent sessions are merged, feature-extracted, and balanced to produce the unified training set.</span></figcaption>

</section>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1. </span>Human Behavioral Data</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We source human interaction data from CaptchaSolve30k <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>)</cite>, a public dataset of mouse dynamics recorded during real CAPTCHA-solving tasks on the HuggingFace Hub. The dataset contains mouse trajectories from over 14,000 sessions, each capturing cursor movements, clicks, and timing as users solve visual CAPTCHAs. Event parsing, click-edge reconstruction, trajectory segmentation, and 60 Hz resampling details are given in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Dataset Processing Details ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2. </span>Synthetic Bot Generation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Real bot traffic is difficult to obtain at scale with ground-truth labels. We generate synthetic bot data using a three-archetype model that reflects the real-world spectrum of bot sophistication <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>)</cite>:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Headless bots</span> (35% of samples) model browser automation without a visible browser window <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>)</cite>. These bots produce no mouse, scroll, or keyboard events; 85% expose the <span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">navigator.webdriver</span> flag; and 70% report zero viewport dimensions.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Scripted bots</span> (35%) model Selenium/Puppeteer-driven automation with basic mouse simulation. They produce low trajectory entropy (<math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{N}(0.5,0.3)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{N}(0.5,0.3)</annotation></semantics></math>), high movement efficiency (<math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{N}(0.92,0.05)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.92</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.05</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{N}(0.92,0.05)</annotation></semantics></math>), fast uniform clicks (<math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{N}(50,15)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>15</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{N}(50,15)</annotation></semantics></math> ms mean duration), and high teleport-click ratios (<math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{N}(0.55,0.2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.55</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{N}(0.55,0.2)</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Sophisticated bots</span> (30%) model behavior-mimicking automation with deliberate humanization. Their distributions intentionally overlap with human behavior: trajectory entropy <math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{N}(1.8,0.6)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1.8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.6</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{N}(1.8,0.6)</annotation></semantics></math>, click duration <math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{N}(85,25)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>85</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>25</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{N}(85,25)</annotation></semantics></math> ms, and inter-event entropy <math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{N}(2.5,0.7)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2.5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.7</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{N}(2.5,0.7)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">All features are drawn from clipped normal distributions to ensure physical plausibility (e.g., non-negative durations, efficiencies in <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>). Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.2. Synthetic Bot Generation ‣ 3. Dataset Construction ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes the distribution parameters for all archetypes alongside the human baseline.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S3.T1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>. </span><span id="S3.T1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Distribution parameters for synthetic bot generation. </table>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We generate 5,000 synthetic bot samples balanced across the three archetypes. The sophisticated archetype is deliberately designed to overlap with human distributions, making the bot-vs-human boundary the hardest classification challenge, an important design choice: it ensures our detector cannot rely on trivially separable features.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3. </span>Agent Data Collection</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We collect real AI agent behavioral data using Claude <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>)</cite> driving a Chrome browser via the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The agent performs web tasks spanning <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">five interaction types</span>: (i) form interaction, (ii) navigation &amp; reading, (iii) authentication, (iv) UI widget selection, and (v) multi-step input flows, instantiated across 10 concrete task instances:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="S3.I2" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S3.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(1)</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Form filling</span> (httpbin.org/forms/post): <em id="S3.I2.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">form interaction</em></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(2)</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Search navigation</span> (Google search): <em id="S3.I2.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">navigation &amp; reading</em></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(3)</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multi-page reading</span> (Wikipedia with 3 link clicks): <em id="S3.I2.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">navigation &amp; reading</em></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(4)</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Login flow</span> (the-internet.herokuapp.com/login): <em id="S3.I2.i4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">authentication</em></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(5)</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Dropdown &amp; checkbox selection</span>: <em id="S3.I2.i5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">UI widget selection</em></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i6" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(6)</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Table reading</span> (row interaction): <em id="S3.I2.i6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">navigation &amp; reading</em></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i7" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(7)</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i7.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Infinite scrolling</span>: <em id="S3.I2.i7.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">navigation &amp; reading</em></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i8" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(8)</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i8.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i8.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Text input</span> (TinyMCE editor): <em id="S3.I2.i8.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">multi-step input flows</em></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i9" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(9)</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i9.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i9.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i9.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Drag and drop</span>: <em id="S3.I2.i9.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">UI widget selection</em></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i10" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(10)</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i10.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i10.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i10.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multi-step wizard</span> (demoqa.com): <em id="S3.I2.i10.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">multi-step input flows</em></p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Each session is recorded as a JSONL event stream capturing all DOM events (<span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mousemove</span>, <span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mousedown</span>, <span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mouseup</span>, <span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">click</span>, <span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">keydown</span>, <span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">keyup</span>, <span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">scroll</span>) with timestamps and the <span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">isTrusted</span> flag. We collect 1,025 agent sessions across all task types.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4. </span>Dataset Unification</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We merge the three data sources into a unified dataset with consistent label encoding: 0 = human, 1 = bot, 2 = agent. All bot archetypes (headless, scripted, sophisticated) map to label 1. The merged pool contains <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">6,025 rows</span> (3,000 human, 2,000 bot, 1,025 agent) represented by <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">29 columns</span>: 17 continuous behavioral features (the original 16 plus <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">scroll_interval_variance</span>, which cleanly separates inter-scroll timing from wheel-delta magnitude after we fixed a previous mislabeling in the resampler; see Methodology), 7 binary environment features, and 5 metadata columns (<span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">label</span>, <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">archetype</span>, <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">source</span>, <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">task_name</span>, <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">session_id</span>). Five of the 17 continuous features (<span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">teleport_click_ratio</span>, <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">scroll_speed_variance</span>, <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">inter_action_gap_variance</span>, <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">inter_action_gap_bimodality</span>, <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">time_to_first_action</span>) are agent-specific by design (§<a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1. Agent-Specific Feature Hypotheses ‣ 4. Feature Engineering ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>). To prevent class imbalance from biasing the classifier, we apply stratified downsampling (<span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.14" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">balance_dataset</span>) to the size of the smallest class, producing a balanced training pool of <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.15" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3,075 rows</span> (1,025 per class) with fixed seed (<math id="S3.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> = 42). All three-class experiments use this balanced pool with a 70/15/15 train/val/test split (<math id="S3.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>462 test samples per seed, <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>154 per class).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4. </span>Feature Engineering</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We extract 17 continuous behavioral features and 7 binary environment features from each session’s event stream. The continuous features fall into four categories: trajectory (entropy, movement efficiency, teleportation count, path linearity), click (duration mean and standard deviation), timing (event rate, inter-event entropy, action-gap statistics, typing speed), and agent-specific ratios (<span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">teleport_click_ratio</span>, <span id="S4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">scroll_speed_variance</span>). Formal definitions for every feature are given in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Feature Definitions ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>. All continuous features are min-max normalized with statistics fitted on the training split only, and nullable features carry paired missingness indicators (<span id="S4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">has_*</span>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1. </span>Agent-Specific Feature Hypotheses</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We hypothesize that LLM-driven agents exhibit a characteristic <em id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">pause-think-act</em> cycle that distinguishes them from both humans (continuous, variable interaction) and traditional bots (uniform, mechanical interaction). During the “pause” phase, the agent waits for the LLM to process page content; during “think,” the LLM generates a plan; during “act,” the agent executes a burst of browser commands. This produces a bimodal distribution of inter-action gaps: short gaps (<math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&lt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;</annotation></semantics></math>1 s) within action bursts and long gaps (<math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&gt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;</annotation></semantics></math>1 s) during LLM inference.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The features <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">inter_action_gap_variance</span>, <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">inter_action_gap_bimodality</span>, <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">action_burst_ratio</span>, and <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">time_to_first_action</span> are specifically designed to capture this signal. All agent-specific features are nullable: set to <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">None</span> if a session contains insufficient action events for reliable estimation.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Empirical caveat.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">None of these four hypothesis-driven features survive backward elimination (§<a href="#S9" title="9. Feature Subset Optimization ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>): <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">inter_action_gap_variance</span>, <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">action_burst_ratio</span>, <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">inter_action_gap_bimodality</span>, and <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">time_to_first_action</span> are all removed by step 10 without any drop in agent recall. The surviving 2-feature necessary set {<span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">mouse_event_rate</span>, <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">click_duration_std</span>} contains no cognition-correlated feature. This suggests that while the pause-think-act hypothesis is directionally interesting, the discriminative signal in practice is carried by event-stream structure (the overall rate of raw mousemove emissions and the near-zero variance of click hold times), which encodes API-level execution artifacts rather than LLM inference patterns specifically.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2. </span>Binary Environment Features</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Seven binary features capture browser environment signals: <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">no_mouse_events</span>, <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">no_scroll_events</span>, <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">no_keyboard_events</span> (absence of entire event categories), <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">zero_dimensions</span> (zero viewport), <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">webdriver_flag</span> (<span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">navigator.webdriver</span>), <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">has_untrusted_events</span> (any event with <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">isTrusted</span>=false), and <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">no_micro_jitter</span> (absence of sub-pixel cursor movements during rest). These are excluded from subset analysis because they are trivially spoofable by setting browser properties.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5. </span>Model Architecture</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We adapt the SAINT tabular transformer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>)</cite> for three-class classification: each continuous feature is embedded through its own linear projection (<math id="S5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> = 32), each binary feature through a learned lookup, a learnable CLS token is prepended, and two transformer blocks (4 attention heads) feed a task-specific classification head (binary or three-class). The encoder is pre-trained with a denoising objective (30% feature masking) before supervised fine-tuning. Figure <a href="#A3.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ Early Stopping. ‣ C.7. Training Procedure ‣ Appendix C SAINT Architecture and Training Details ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C SAINT Architecture and Training Details ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> shows the full pipeline; architectural equations, the training procedure, and all hyperparameters (Table <a href="#A3.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ Early Stopping. ‣ C.7. Training Procedure ‣ Appendix C SAINT Architecture and Training Details ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>) are given there.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1. </span>Threat Model</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider an attacker who controls a browser automation agent and seeks to evade detection as “human” while completing web tasks. The attacker has <em id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">white-box</em> knowledge of the feature set (all 16 continuous + 7 binary features) but only <em id="S5.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">black-box</em> access to the detection model: they cannot inspect model weights or gradients. The attacker operates through a browser automation API (Playwright) and cannot inject events at the OS level or use hardware input devices. We define five escalating evasion levels with increasing attacker sophistication (Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Evasion Methodology ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2. </span>Experimental Protocol</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All experiments use a 70/15/15 stratified train/validation/test split. For the binary detection gap experiment (§<a href="#S6" title="6. The Binary Detection Gap ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>), we train on 5,000 human+bot samples and evaluate on the held-out test set plus all 1,025 agent sessions. For three-class experiments, we train on the unified balanced dataset. For feature subset optimization (§<a href="#S9" title="9. Feature Subset Optimization ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>), we use GradientBoosting classifiers (100 estimators, max_depth = 4) for computational efficiency, as evaluating 9,401 subsets with SAINT would be prohibitive.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To ensure statistical robustness, we evaluate all three-class results across 10 random seeds (<math id="S5.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> = 42…51), each producing a different balanced subsample and train/val/test split, and report mean <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> standard deviation with 95% confidence intervals (§<a href="#S10" title="10. Multi-Seed Evaluation ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>). We additionally perform a task-domain ablation (§<a href="#S8" title="8. Task-Domain Ablation ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>) to control for potential confounds between human and agent data sources before proceeding to feature optimization.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6. </span>The Binary Detection Gap</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Existing bot detectors assume a binary world: human or bot. To evaluate whether this suffices for agents, we train four binary classifiers (human vs. bot) on 5,000 human+bot samples and evaluate on 1,025 agent sessions. Since these detectors have no “agent” class, each agent is classified as either human (evasion) or bot (detection).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S6.T2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 2</span>. </span><span id="S6.T2.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Binary bot detectors evaluated on AI agent traffic. The MLP is the most vulnerable, letting 39.1% of agents through as “human”; SAINT is close behind at 34.5%. XGBoost achieves 100% detection, but via coincidental features (missing scroll events, empty raw mousemove streams before clicks, absent <span id="S6.T2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">wheel</span> events) rather than agent-specific signals; see §<a href="#S6" title="6. The Binary Detection Gap ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.</span></figcaption>
<table id="S6.T2.6" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="S6.T2.6.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S6.T2.6.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt"><span id="S6.T2.6.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Detector</span></th>
<th id="S6.T2.6.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="S6.T2.6.1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Evasion</span></th>
<th id="S6.T2.6.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="S6.T2.6.1.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Detection</span></th>
<th id="S6.T2.6.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="S6.T2.6.1.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Mean <math id="S6.T2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\text{bot}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>bot</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\text{bot}}</annotation></semantics></math></span></th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S6.T2.6.2" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S6.T2.6.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t"><span id="S6.T2.6.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">MLP</span></th>
<td id="S6.T2.6.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t"><span id="S6.T2.6.2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">39.1%</span></td>
<td id="S6.T2.6.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t"><span id="S6.T2.6.2.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">60.9%</span></td>
<td id="S6.T2.6.2.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t"><span id="S6.T2.6.2.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">0.633</span></td></tr>

<td id="S6.T2.6.3.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S6.T2.6.3.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">0.633</span></td></tr>

<td id="S6.T2.6.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S6.T2.6.4.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">30.0%</span></td>

<td id="S6.T2.6.4.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S6.T2.6.4.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">0.548</span></td></tr>
