<td id="S6.T2.6.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S6.T2.6.5.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">0.0%</span></td>
<td id="S6.T2.6.5.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S6.T2.6.5.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">100.0%</span></td>
<td id="S6.T2.6.5.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S6.T2.6.5.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">0.904</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S6.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 6. The Binary Detection Gap ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> reveals a critical gap. The MLP binary classifier is <em id="S6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">the most vulnerable</em>, allowing 39.1% of agents through as “human”; the SAINT transformer is nearly as exposed at 34.5%. Their mean <math id="S6.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\text{bot}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>bot</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\text{bot}}</annotation></semantics></math> on agent samples is only 0.633, barely above the 0.5 threshold.<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
          Low confidence near the decision boundary is expected for out-of-distribution inputs that fall between the learned human and bot clusters, and does not indicate that agents are genuinely human-like: it reflects the absence of an agent class in the binary model’s output space.</span></span></span> XGBoost <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>)</cite> catches 100% of agents, but does so via coincidental features (missing scroll events, missing raw-event teleports, absent mousemove streams before clicks) rather than agent-specific signals, making the “detection” brittle in exactly the way §<a href="#S9" title="9. Feature Subset Optimization ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> will show.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The fix is simple: add a third class.</span> When trained on human+bot+agent data, the same SAINT architecture achieves F1 = 1.000 for agents across all 10 seeds (§<a href="#S10" title="10. Multi-Seed Evaluation ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>). The 34.5% gap vanishes entirely. This establishes that (a) the binary setup cannot reliably detect agents <em id="S6.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">as a class</em> (MLP and SAINT, the strongest human/bot boundary learners, fail on 39.1% and 34.5%, respectively, while models that do catch agents rely on brittle, non-agent-specific signals) and (b) a purpose-built three-class detector solves the problem.<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
            
            
            
          When we say binary detectors “cannot detect agents,” we mean the binary label space cannot <em id="footnote2.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">represent</em> a three-class world: this is a representational limitation, not a modeling one. A binary detector trained with agents labeled as bots would of course classify them as bots, but would then lose the ability to route agents as a distinct traffic class.</span></span></span> This motivates our investigation into which features a three-class detector actually needs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7. </span>Evasion Ladder</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We define five levels of escalating attacker capability, from unmodified browser automation to replay of real human behavioral data (detailed methodology in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Evasion Methodology ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Level 1 (None):</span> The agent uses Playwright’s native API with no modifications: cursor teleports, clicks complete in <math id="S7.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&lt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;</annotation></semantics></math>2 ms, actions burst between LLM inference pauses.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Level 2 (Rule-based):</span> Bézier-curve cursor paths, human-sampled click durations (60–180 ms), and random inter-action delays (500–2000 ms). See Appendix <a href="#A4.SS1" title="D.1. Rule-Based Evasion (Level 2) ‣ Appendix D Evasion Methodology ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Level 3 (GAN):</span> A conditional WGAN-GP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>)</cite> trained on 14,342 real human trajectory segments generates mouse paths conditioned on distance, angle, and duration. See Appendix <a href="#A4.SS2" title="D.2. Conditional WGAN-GP (Levels 3–4) ‣ Appendix D Evasion Methodology ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Level 4 (GAN+):</span> GAN trajectories augmented with Gaussian micro-jitter (<math id="S7.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> = 1.5 px), Fitts-law timing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>)</cite>, and human-sampled click/gap distributions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Level 5 (Human Replay):</span> Real human trajectories from CaptchaSolve30k <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>)</cite>, warped via KD-tree matching <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>)</cite> to fit required movements. LLM inference is decoupled from action execution. See Appendix <a href="#A4.SS3" title="D.3. Human Trajectory Replay (Level 5) ‣ Appendix D Evasion Methodology ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S7.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S7.T3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 3</span>. </span><span id="S7.T3.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Five-level evasion ladder. The SAINT-3class detector achieves 100% detection at all levels with near-maximum confidence.<sup id="S7.T3.5.1" class="ltx_sup">†</sup> All five levels operate within Playwright-mediated automation; see §<a href="#S7" title="7. Evasion Ladder ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> and the Limitations paragraph in §<a href="#S12" title="12. Discussion &amp; Conclusion ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> for discussion of evasion paths outside this scope.</span></figcaption>

<div id="S7.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S7.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 7. Evasion Ladder ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows the central result: <span id="S7.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">100% agent detection at all five evasion levels</span> within Playwright-mediated automation (<math id="S7.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> = 524 replay sessions, up from the 165 cited in prior versions; the loader is now shared between replay and feature-optimization experiments via <span id="S7.p7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">bot_detector.data.evasion.load_replay_evaluation_set</span>, eliminating a prior count discrepancy). No agent session at any level is misclassified. Even replay of real human trajectories with human-sampled timing fails to evade: the final click is still <span id="S7.p7.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">element.click()</span> dispatched without preceding mouse motion, and scroll events are still emitted by a programmatic event loop rather than a physical wheel or trackpad. This produces three concrete artifacts that evasion at the cursor-path level cannot mask: (i) clicks with no preceding raw <span id="S7.p7.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mousemove</span> stream terminating at the target (0 of 1,025 normal agent sessions contain a raw-event teleport before any click; 0 of 524 replay sessions do either, under the raw-event definition of <span id="S7.p7.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">teleport_click_ratio</span>), (ii) complete absence of <span id="S7.p7.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">wheel</span> events so that <span id="S7.p7.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">scroll_speed_var</span> is unobservable (null in 1,025/1,025 normal agent sessions), and (iii) highly regular inter-scroll timing when scrolls <em id="S7.p7.1.8" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">are</em> dispatched, from synchronous event-loop delivery. These absence and regularity artifacts are surfaced to the classifier through explicit missingness-indicator columns (<span id="S7.p7.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">has_*</span>) emitted alongside each continuous feature; they are robust to any evasion method that operates within Playwright’s public API. Evasion methods that bypass browser automation APIs entirely, such as OS-level input simulation (e.g., xdotool, PyAutoGUI), hardware mouse emulators, or CDP-level event injection configured to synthesize hardware-style event streams, are outside our threat model (§<a href="#S5.SS1" title="5.1. Threat Model ‣ 5. Model Architecture ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.1</span></a>) and would likely require different detection approaches. Before investigating which features carry these signals, we first address the strongest potential confound.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">8. </span>Task-Domain Ablation</h2>

<div id="S8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A critical threat to validity: our human data comes from CAPTCHA-solving sessions (CaptchaSolve30k <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>)</cite>), which contain mouse-only interactions: no typing, no scrolling, no multi-page navigation. Agent data spans 10 diverse web tasks including forms, login flows, scrolling, and text input. Several features could therefore act as task proxies rather than agent signals: <span id="S8.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">typing_speed</span> is null for all humans, <span id="S8.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">scroll_speed_var</span> is zero, and binary flags like <span id="S8.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">no_keyboard_events</span> directly encode whether the session involved typing. If the detector merely learns “sessions with typing are agents,” our results would be vacuous.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To test whether detection survives without these confounds, we define three feature tiers:</p>
<ul id="S8.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S8.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S8.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">All features</span>: the original 16 continuous + 7 binary (baseline).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S8.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S8.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Task-agnostic</span>: 9 continuous features present in both CAPTCHA and web tasks (trajectory entropy, movement efficiency, mouse teleportation, mouse event rate, teleport-click ratio, click duration mean/std, inter-event entropy, cursor path linearity) + 5 non-task-correlated binary features. Excludes typing speed, scroll speed variance, and all agent gap features.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S8.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S8.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Task-agnostic, no binary</span>: the 9 task-agnostic continuous features only, with all binary environment features removed.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="S8.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S8.T4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 4</span>. </span><span id="S8.T4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Task-domain ablation. Removing task-correlated features has zero impact on agent detection; macro-F1 drops slightly due to harder bot/human separation. P/R columns show per-class precision and recall.</span></figcaption>

<div id="S8.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S8.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 8. Task-Domain Ablation ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> settles the question: <span id="S8.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">agent detection is invariant to feature tier</span>. Agent F1 remains 1.000 across all three tiers for both SAINT and GBM. The evasion ladder likewise shows 100% detection at all five levels under the task-agnostic-no-binary tier. Macro-F1 drops by <math id="S8.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>1% when task-correlated features are removed, reflecting a slightly harder bot-vs-human boundary, but the agent detection signal is entirely carried by task-agnostic mouse dynamics features, not by task identity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p4.1" class="ltx_p">This confirms that the discriminating signal (cursor teleportation patterns, click timing, event-stream entropy) is a property of <em id="S8.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">how automation APIs generate events</em>, not an artifact of what tasks the sessions contain. With this confound addressed, we proceed to identify the minimal features needed.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S9" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">9. </span>Feature Subset Optimization</h2>

<div id="S9.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given that detection is robust across all evasion levels, we ask: what is the <em id="S9.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">minimal</em> set of features needed? We evaluate every feature subset on two criteria: perfect agent detection (100% at all 5 evasion levels) and macro-F1 across 3 classes.</p>
</div>
<section id="S9.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Methodology.</h4>

<div id="S9.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For computational tractability, we use GradientBoosting classifiers (100 estimators, max_depth = 4) rather than SAINT for the exhaustive search, as training 9,401 SAINT models would be prohibitive. We note that the subset results reported below are therefore GBM-specific; the headline claims are validated with SAINT on the identified minimal subsets in Table <a href="#S9.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ SAINT validation on minimal subsets. ‣ 9.2. Backward Elimination ‣ 9. Feature Subset Optimization ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>. Binary environment features are included as a fixed baseline in all subsets, since they provide unambiguous detection signals but are trivially spoofable; the subset analysis focuses on the 17 continuous behavioral features. Macro-F1 is reported on the <em id="S9.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">held-out test split</em> (not the training data), so all values in Tables <a href="#S9.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 9.1. Exhaustive Search ‣ 9. Feature Subset Optimization ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> and <a href="#S9.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 9.2. Backward Elimination ‣ 9. Feature Subset Optimization ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> are out-of-sample. For forward selection we use a composite score: <math id="S9.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{score}=\bar{r}_{\text{detect}}+0.01\cdot F1_{\text{macro}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>score</mtext><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mtext>detect</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>0.01</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>F</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mn>1</mn><mtext>macro</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{score}=\bar{r}_{\text{detect}}+0.01\cdot F1_{\text{macro}}</annotation></semantics></math>, which prioritizes detection rate and uses F1 as a tiebreaker.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S9.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">9.1. </span>Exhaustive Search</h3>

<div id="S9.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We enumerate all <math id="S9.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\binom{17}{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mn>17</mn><mi>k</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\binom{17}{k}</annotation></semantics></math> feature subsets for <math id="S9.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> = 1…5, training a classifier on each and evaluating against all evasion levels.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S9.T5" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S9.T5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 5</span>. </span><span id="S9.T5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Exhaustive search results over 9,401 GBM trainings. “Perfect” subsets are those achieving 100% agent detection at all 5 evasion levels on held-out test data. Best F1 is held-out test macro-F1 (not training F1). At <math id="S9.T5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> = 1 only a single subset is “perfect,” but it is a degenerate all-agent predictor; genuine three-class discrimination starts at <math id="S9.T5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> = 2.</span></figcaption>

</figure>
<figure id="S9.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2607.26935v1/fig1_exhaustive_search.png" id="S9.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/257;" width="476" height="257" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S9.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>. </span><span id="S9.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Exhaustive search: total subsets tested vs. subsets achieving perfect agent detection. At <math id="S9.F2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> = 1, only 3/16 features suffice solo; the fraction grows rapidly with <math id="S9.F2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S9.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S9.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 9.1. Exhaustive Search ‣ 9. Feature Subset Optimization ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> and Figure <a href="#S9.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 9.1. Exhaustive Search ‣ 9. Feature Subset Optimization ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> reveal that “perfect” agent detection at <math id="S9.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> = 1 is essentially an artifact of the evaluation: the single solo-perfect feature <span id="S9.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">cursor_path_linearity</span> is a missingness-style indicator that equals 1 for all 1,025 normal agent sessions, all 2,299 evasion sessions, and almost no human or bot sessions. A GBM trained on this one column learns “always predict agent” and therefore catches every agent (recall = 1.00) at the cost of flagging every human and bot (agent precision = 0.33, macro-F1 = 0.17, ROC-AUC = 0.50 against a balanced non-agent set). This is caught automatically by the per-level diagnostics introduced below; we report it as the baseline but do not count it as a deployable detector.</p>
</div>
<div id="S9.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Genuine three-class discrimination with 100% agent recall starts at <math id="S9.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> = 2. The best <math id="S9.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> = 2 perfect subset is {<span id="S9.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">mouse_event_rate</span>, <span id="S9.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">teleport_click_ratio</span>}, which achieves held-out macro-F1 = 0.926 with agent precision = 0.994 and ROC-AUC = 1.000 at every evasion level.<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
              
              
              
            On our regenerated features, <span id="footnote3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">teleport_click_ratio</span> is the fraction of clicks preceded within 100 ms by a raw-event mousemove jump of <math id="footnote3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&gt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;</annotation></semantics></math>100 px and <math id="footnote3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&lt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;</annotation></semantics></math>50 ms, a definition that matches the feature’s name. Under that definition it is exactly <math id="footnote3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> for all 1,025 Playwright-driven agent sessions, which is why it contributes: combined with <span id="footnote3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">mouse_event_rate</span> (non-null but sparse for agents), the classifier separates agents through the empty-teleport signature rather than through any positive value of the ratio.</span></span></span> At <math id="S9.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> = 3, 51 of 680 subsets are perfect (7.5%); at <math id="S9.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> = 5, 1,168 of 6,188 (18.9%). The best held-out test macro-F1 climbs from 0.952 (<math id="S9.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> = 2) through 0.974, 0.987, to 0.991 (<math id="S9.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> = 5), indicating that five features are required to push the bot-vs-human boundary (which is intrinsically harder than the agent boundary) to <math id="S9.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\geq 0.99" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≥</mo><mn>0.99</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\geq 0.99</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S9.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Countermeasure: neutralizing <span id="S9.SS1.SSS0.Px1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">teleport_click_ratio</span>.</h4>

<div id="S9.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A Playwright scripter who reads this paper might ask: what if I precede every <span id="S9.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">page.click()</span> with a <span id="S9.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">page.mouse.move()</span> to the target, producing a nonzero <span id="S9.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">teleport_click_ratio</span>? We test the strongest version of this countermeasure (removing <span id="S9.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">teleport_click_ratio</span> from the feature set entirely) across 10 seeds. Full-feature GBM macro-F1 is essentially unchanged (<math id="S9.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.996\pm 0.003" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.996</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>0.003</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.996\pm 0.003</annotation></semantics></math> with all features vs. <math id="S9.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.994\pm 0.004" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.994</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>0.004</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.994\pm 0.004</annotation></semantics></math> without it) and agent recall remains 100% in every seed. Backward elimination on the full 17-feature set (§<a href="#S9.SS2" title="9.2. Backward Elimination ‣ 9. Feature Subset Optimization ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9.2</span></a>) removes <span id="S9.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">teleport_click_ratio</span> at step 9 without any drop in detection, and the surviving 2-feature necessary set {<span id="S9.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">mouse_event_rate</span>, <span id="S9.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">click_duration_std</span>} contains neither teleport nor scroll features. The signal is redundantly encoded across <span id="S9.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">mouse_event_rate</span>, <span id="S9.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">click_duration_std</span>, <span id="S9.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">typing_speed_std</span>, and the missingness-indicator channels for scroll and keyboard: neutralizing any single feature does not rescue the agent.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S9.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Forward selection.</h4>

<div id="S9.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Greedy forward selection terminates in a single step selecting <span id="S9.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">cursor_path_linearity</span>, precisely because that one column gives 100% “detection” by collapsing the predictor. Because the forward-selection scorer weights detection rate over F1, it cannot see past this degenerate one-feature solution; the exhaustive search above and the backward elimination below are what identify the minimal <em id="S9.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">deployable</em> subsets.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S9.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2607.26935v1/fig2_forward_selection.png" id="S9.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/258;" width="476" height="258" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S9.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>. </span><span id="S9.F3.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Forward selection trajectory. The greedy search terminates in a single step after adding <span id="S9.F3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">teleport_click_ratio</span>, which already achieves 100% agent detection at all five evasion levels.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S9.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">9.2. </span>Backward Elimination</h3>

<div id="S9.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Starting from all 17 continuous features (F1 = 0.987, 100% agent detection at every evasion level), we greedily remove the feature whose removal least affects held-out test macro-F1 and preserves 100% agent detection. Table <a href="#S9.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 9.2. Backward Elimination ‣ 9. Feature Subset Optimization ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> shows the elimination sequence; Figure <a href="#S9.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 9.2. Backward Elimination ‣ 9. Feature Subset Optimization ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> visualizes the full F1 trajectory as features are removed.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S9.T6" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S9.T6.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 6</span>. </span><span id="S9.T6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Backward elimination on the 17 continuous features. Features removed in order of least impact on held-out test macro-F1 (with 100% agent detection at every evasion level preserved as a hard constraint). Detection breaks only at step 16 when the penultimate feature is removed, leaving a single column.</span></figcaption>

<tfoot class="ltx_tfoot">
<tr id="S9.T6.5.19" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S9.T6.5.19.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt" colspan="4"><sup id="S9.T6.5.19.1.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S9.T6.5.19.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">†</span></sup><span id="S9.T6.5.19.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;"> Breaks: <span id="S9.T6.5.19.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">none</span>-level detection drops to 70%</span></th></tr>
<tr id="S9.T6.5.20" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S9.T6.5.20.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row" colspan="4"><span id="S9.T6.5.20.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">({<span id="S9.T6.5.20.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:129%;">mouse_event_rate</span>} alone).</span></th></tr>
</tfoot>
</table>
</figure>
<figure id="S9.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2607.26935v1/fig3_backward_elimination.png" id="S9.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/235;" width="476" height="235" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S9.F4.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>. </span><span id="S9.F4.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Backward elimination: held-out test macro-F1 vs. number of features remaining. The green zone indicates 100% agent detection at every evasion level; the red zone indicates degraded performance. The 2-feature necessary set {<span id="S9.F4.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mouse_event_rate</span>, <span id="S9.F4.6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">click_duration_std</span>} holds both 100% agent recall and unit agent precision; dropping to 1 feature is the only step that breaks detection on the “none” level.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S9.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">15 of the 17 continuous features can be removed without ever breaking the 100% agent-recall invariant. The first 8 removals (scroll_interval_variance, trajectory_entropy, inter_event_entropy, movement_efficiency, inter_action_gap_variance, cursor_path_linearity, inter_action_gap_bimodality, action_burst_ratio) actually <em id="S9.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">improve</em> held-out F1 from 0.987 to 0.996 by reducing overfitting. F1 degrades gracefully as elimination continues, dipping below 0.99 at 5 features and below 0.95 at 2. Only at step 16, when only <span id="S9.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">mouse_event_rate</span> remains, does the detection invariant break: “none”-level detection drops to 70% because a single mouse-event-rate threshold cannot distinguish agents from the human tail.</p>
</div>
<div id="S9.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The <span id="S9.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2 necessary features</span> for 100% agent detection under GBM, <em id="S9.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">given a three-class formulation</em>, are:</p>
<ul id="S9.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S9.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S9.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S9.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">mouse_event_rate</span>: rate (events/second) of mousemove events in the session</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S9.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S9.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S9.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">click_duration_std</span>: standard deviation of mousedown-to-mouseup durations</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S9.SS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">Together they yield held-out test macro-F1 = 0.904, Agent precision = 1.000, Agent recall = 1.000, and 100% detection at all five evasion levels (ROC-AUC = 1.000 against the mixed held-out set at every level). Five features push macro-F1 above 0.99 (Table <a href="#S9.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 9.1. Exhaustive Search ‣ 9. Feature Subset Optimization ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>), and 17 features reach 0.995 (Table <a href="#S10.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ 10. Multi-Seed Evaluation ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>); the incremental benefit of features 3–17 is almost entirely in the human–bot boundary, not in agent detection.</p>
</div>
<section id="S9.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">SAINT validation on minimal subsets.</h4>

<div id="S9.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Because our exhaustive search uses GBM for tractability, we re-train SAINT on the <math id="S9.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> = 2 best-perfect exhaustive subset, the 2-feature backward-elimination necessary set, and the <math id="S9.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> = 5 best exhaustive subset (3 seeds each, all five evasion levels). All three subsets preserve SAINT agent recall = 1.000 at every evasion level. SAINT macro-F1 trails GBM by roughly 0.01–0.03 on small subsets (expected, given SAINT’s higher parameter count and the small training budget of 30 epochs), but the agent-detection invariant is classifier-agnostic.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S9.T7" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S9.T7.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 7</span>. </span><span id="S9.T7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">SAINT validation on minimal subsets identified by the GBM search (<math id="S9.T7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> = 3 seeds, 30 epochs, patience 5). Training budget is lighter than the main protocol (Table <a href="#A3.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ Early Stopping. ‣ C.7. Training Procedure ‣ Appendix C SAINT Architecture and Training Details ‣ What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>) because this is a validation experiment. Values are mean over seeds; evasion levels report agent-detection rate.</span></figcaption>

<section id="S10" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">10. </span>Multi-Seed Evaluation</h2>

<div id="S10.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S10.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To verify statistical stability, we repeat all three-class experiments across 10 random seeds (<math id="S10.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> = 42…51), each producing a different balanced subsample and 70/15/15 train/val/test split (<math id="S10.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>462 test samples per seed, <math id="S10.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>154 per class).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S10.T8" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S10.T8.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 8</span>. </span><span id="S10.T8.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Multi-seed evaluation (<math id="S10.T8.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> = 10 seeds). Agent F1 = 1.000 across all 30 runs (3 models <math id="S10.T8.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> 10 seeds). 95% CIs computed via the <math id="S10.T8.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>-distribution. P/R are mean per-class precision/recall.</span></figcaption>
